newsitem.title: USA: Marvel shares slide after forecast, deal.
newsitem.headline: Marvel shares slide after forecast, deal.

text.p: Shares of comic book publisher Marvel Entertainment Group Inc fell 1-7/8 points to 2-3/4 after the company reported a third quarter loss and received a restructuring proposal that would merge its operations with Toy Biz Inc.
"Marvel Entertainment will no longer be a bankruptcy candidate," John Kyle Cartwright, high-yield bond analyst at Wheat First Butcher Singer, said about the deal.

Financier Ronald Perelman's Andrews Group offered to merge the operations of Toy Biz with Marvel, which is 80 percent owned by Perelman holding companies. The $350 million deal would keep Perelman's holdings of Marvel, which does not meed its financial covenants and expects a fourth quarter loss, at approximately 80 percent

David Leibowitz, a managing director at Burnham Securities, said, "The announcements of today were clearly not well received by many Marvel investors. The stock's price action would indicated that the proposed transaction is very much not to their liking."
Leibowitz, however, said Marvel's outside directors may change some of the terms of the proposal.

However, the deal will involve the issuance of more than 400 million shares of common stock, in addition to the 100 million shares presently outstanding. A Perelman holding company agreed to buy 67 percent of Toy Biz's class A common shares last month.
The proposal also could hurt bondholders, said Cartwright, who said he is unhappy with the deal. He acknowledged that the Toy Biz deal will make Marvel a stronger operating company.

The deal could let Perelman's holding companies that control Marvel Entertainment walk away from nearly $900 million in debt in exchange for his $350 million investment in Toy Biz Inc, Cartwright said.

A spokesman for Perelman's Andrews Group, which is proposing the Toy Biz deal, said the alternative to the Toy Biz deal might have been bankruptcy and that would have hurt Marvel investors further and that Perelman is adding to his own risk by investing the $350 million.
The bonds through various holding companies controlled by Perelman are secured by Marvel common stock that would be significantly diluted if the Toy Biz deal were completed.
"If Marvel entertainment were to earn $50 million next year on 500 million shares, that's $0.10 a share," Cartwright said about the dilution involved with this proposal.
Cartwright noted that even if Marvel were valued at 20 times its earnings, the stock would be worth $2 a share under that scenario.

Bond markets may make Perelman pay a steeper price to complete future deals. "This is going to cost him (Perelman) one or two hundred basis points in interest costs for future deals," Cartwright said.
